reconcile.connective: Commentators read Jonah 2:3 as ascribing to God, as first cause, what the sailors carried out in 1:15 as his reluctant instruments.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain wording as a genuine contradiction: one verse names the sailors, the other names God, as the one who cast Jonah in.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (skepticsannotatedbible.com, est. 1999; print ed. 2013)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Though the mariners did this, yet Jonah ascribes it to the Lord; he knew it was he, whom he had sinned against and offended … and overcame the reluctance of the men to it, and so worked upon them that they did it; and therefore Jonah imputes it to him, and not to them …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States plainly that the sailors physically threw Jonah, but Jonah's own prayer imputes the act to God, who overcame their reluctance and worked through them — the secondary-causation resolution of the two verses.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Jehovah cast him into the depth of the sea, because the seamen were merely the executors of the punishment inflicted upon him by Jehovah.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes 1:15 and 2:3 by naming the sailors as Jehovah's executors, so 'God cast him' and 'the sailors cast him' describe the same act at two causal levels.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Treats this exact passage: Jonah 2:3's 'Thou castedst me' is explained as Jehovah acting through the sailors of 1:15 as his executors. (Haley's Alleged Discrepancies does not cover this specific verse pair, so the harmonizing commentator already surfaced on the row is used per the contract's fallback.)
